::: {#rem-surprisal-halvings}
#### Surprisal as halvings of certainty

Start from certainty, [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $1$.
Each halving multiplies the probability by $1/2$.
After $s$ halvings the probability is $(1/2)^s$,
and solving $(1/2)^s = p$ for $s$ gives $s = \log_{1/2} p$.
By @thm-surprisal-log-half, this $s$ is the [surprisal](#def-surprisal) in [bits](#def-bit).
So the surprisal of an [outcome](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-experiment-outcome) is the number of times certainty must be halved to reach the probability of that outcome.
When $p$ is not $(1/2)^k$ for a whole number $k$, the number of halvings is not a whole number. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->

:::
